issues.issue: The Grantor is identified as "DeNovo Productions, a division of DeNovo Music Group, Inc." — a division rather than a legal entity — leaving open which entity actually contracted and can enforce. The Artist, whose execution paragraph 6.01(a) makes a condition of payment, is named nowhere in the preamble as a party.

The Initial Period ends eight months after delivery of "the Master Recordings comprising the Recording Obligation," but the contract defines only a "Minimum Recording Obligation" in paragraph 2.02, leaving "Recording Obligation" undefined. Because the Period runs from delivery rather than a calendar date, the Term has no outer limit if delivery never occurs.

This paragraph grants PRI three options, while paragraph 1 of the 1989 amendment deletes the first sentence and substitutes four options with a fourth Option Period. Which version of the option structure governs, and whether the schedule in 2.02 was correspondingly amended, is open.

The warranty that Artist will perform "exclusively for Grantor and PRI" does not say what activity is captured — recording only, or live and audio-visual performance as well — and it sits against the separate audio-visual exclusivity in paragraph 5.02(a)(i). The scope of the exclusivity is the ambiguous term.

The schedule fixes two Albums for each of the Initial and three Option Periods, whereas paragraph 2 of the 1989 amendment sets the Minimum Recording Obligation for the added fourth Option Period at one Album. The two documents must be reconciled to know the total product commitment.

"To the best of their ability" and "first-class standards for production in the Phonograph Record industry" are undefined performance standards with no benchmark stated. Whether a delivered recording meets them is not measurable from the text.

After enumerating specific grounds on which PRI may disapprove a Composition (defamation, libel, infringement, privacy), the clause adds "subject to Objection for any other legal reason whatsoever in the reasonable opinion of PRI's counsel," a catch-all that swallows the enumerated list. Whether the general words are limited by the specifics is exactly the ejusdem generis question.

Delivery is measured by masters that are "technically satisfactory" and embody Recordings that are "first-class- (as that term is understood in the record industry)" — standards whose content is left to industry usage and to PRI's judgment. Whether that is a technical or a commercial-satisfaction test is the ambiguity.

The obligation to furnish "all information, consents and clearances required" is followed by a long enumerated list closing with "any information required to be submitted to unions, if applicable, guilds or other third parties." Whether the catch-all extends beyond the enumerated categories is open.

Paragraph 3.05 requires mechanical licenses from proprietors of compositions "not subject to compulsory license" to be on "the terms provided in Article 9," but Article 9 by its own words governs Controlled Compositions. The cross-reference cannot be squared with 9.01's stated subject matter.

Paragraph 3.06 bars "live" performances from counting toward the Minimum Recording Obligation without PRI's prior written consent, while paragraph 3 of the 1989 amendment requires the first Album of the first Option Period to be a "Live Album" of Soviet Union concert recordings. Whether 3.06 was displaced only for that Album, or more broadly, must be construed.

The 120-day delivery deadline in 4.01(a) was deleted and replaced by paragraph 4 of the 1989 amendment, which carves the Live Album out with a fixed May 29, 1989 date. Which text governs delivery for each Period cannot be told from this provision alone.

The six-to-ten-month window in 4.01(b) was deleted by paragraph 4 of the 1989 amendment and replaced with fixed dates for the first Option Period's second Album. The provision as written no longer squares with the amended delivery schedule.

Extension depends on the parties agreeing "based on good business judgment and based on Artist's then-existing tour commitments" and on dates being "reasonably extended" — none of which is a standard a court can apply without extrinsic evidence. The provision requires agreement that neither party is obliged to give.

The 60-day grace period says Grantor is not in breach of the delivery obligation, but paragraph 6.01(c) reduces the Advance from the "Final Date," defined as the last date the Album "would otherwise be timely delivered pursuant to paragraph 4.01." Whether the Final Date includes this grace period is unresolved between the two.

The delivery date is "suspended until such time as the parties so agree" on a co-producer, with no outer limit and no mechanism to break a deadlock. The suspension is potentially indefinite and its effect on the Contract Period under 1.01 is unstated.

"Satisfactory completion by Grantor of the procedures in Article 3 and this Article 4" makes delivery turn on an unqualified satisfaction standard — whose satisfaction, and measured how, is not said. The final clause then makes acceptance plus release conclusive, which pulls against the same sentence's non-waiver language.

The bar on commencing recording of any Album until ninety days after delivery of the immediately preceding Album cannot always be squared with paragraph 4.01(a), which requires the first Album of each Option Period to be delivered within 120 days of that Period's commencement. Whether "the first Album" in 4.03 means the first Album of each Period or only the very first Album is the point of collision.

Grantor must object "within thirty (30) days of PRI's notice to Grantor," without saying whether the period runs from the date of the notice or its receipt, and no deadline at all is placed on PRI's giving the notice. Deemed acceptance turns on that unstated trigger.

The paragraph gives PRI a right to object to Grantor's proposed delivery date but states no consequence of an objection, leaving the outcome to be pieced together from 4.04(c). What happens if Grantor itself misses the fifteen-day window is likewise unstated.

The sentence "if the parties do not reach such agreement or if neither party gives notice of the delivery date ... earlier than thirty (30) days prior to the date of initial release" is syntactically tangled, so it is unclear whether the thirty-day qualifier attaches to the notice or to the default. The default deemed delivery date turns on reading that garbled clause.

Paragraph 5.01(a) lets PRI "delay or refrain from doing anyone or more of the foregoing" notwithstanding the agreement, excepting only paragraphs 5.01(c) and 5.01(d), yet 5.01(b)(iii) and 5.01(b)(x) impose affirmative release obligations (top-pop label, compact disc within 120 days). The two cannot both be given full effect.

The out-takes consent right is governed by a chapeau limiting 5.01(b) to "sales of Records in the United States during the Term," so it is unclear whether PRI may exploit out-takes abroad or after the Term free of consent. Paragraph 3.03 meanwhile requires out-takes to be delivered subject to "the terms of paragraph 5.01(b)(i)."

"Couple more than two (2) Master Recordings ... during anyone (1) calendar year" does not say whether the limit counts individual couplings, individual Records, or aggregate uses per year. The measure of the two-recording cap is the ambiguity.

The initial release must be on "a label used by PRI at the time of such release for Recordings of PRI's top 'pop' artists then under exclusive term contract" — "top 'pop' artists" has no defined boundary and the roster changes over time. Whether a given imprint satisfies it is not determinable from the text.

"Premium use" is not defined here and, unlike the neighbouring subparagraphs (iv) and (v), Grantor's consent is not qualified as "not to be unreasonably withheld," inviting an expressio unius reading of an absolute veto. Both the term and the unqualified consent are open to construction.

Grantor's approval right over Artwork is contradicted within the same paragraph by PRI's "sole discretion" over "any matter other than the Album cover layout and the picture or art to be used on the cover." Where trademark, notice and sticker matters intersect with cover layout, the two sentences pull in opposite directions.

The subparagraph obliges PRI to request licensees to use the same Artwork and to instruct them to stop violative sales, but then says "PRI shall have no liability by reason of such sales at any time," which negates the obligation it has just created. The internal contradiction between the duty and the blanket exculpation is the defect.

The editing costs are said not to be "attributable to the applicable Recording Fund provided for in paragraph 6.01 below," but paragraph 6.01 creates Advances and contains no "Recording Fund." The cross-reference points to a mechanism that does not exist in the provision named.

The cap applies only to compilations "consisting entirely of Master Recordings recorded hereunder," so a Greatest Hits Album containing one outside track escapes the limit altogether. The word "entirely" is what the limit turns on.

The provision gives Grantor "five (5) business days" to object and then refers back to "said five (5) day period," so the objection window is described two inconsistent ways in the same paragraph. Which count applies decides whether an objection was timely.

The compact disc release obligation is conditioned on its being "commercially possible," a qualifier with no defined content that leaves the obligation effectively at PRI's assessment. Whether it imposes any enforceable duty is the question.

All of Grantor's protections in 5.01(b) fall away if Grantor has not "Materially fulfilled" its delivery obligations — a standard that is undefined and, on its face, forfeits every protection for any one late Master Recording. The reach of "Materially" and of "any Master Recordings" is the ambiguity.

The provision strings together several sixty- and thirty-day periods so that Grantor's termination notice is due "within thirty (30) days following the expiration of such sixty (60) day period," without making clear whether that is the original release period or PRI's cure period. Its opening condition that Grantor have "fulfilled all of its material obligations hereunder" is likewise unmeasured.

Grantor must obtain "all consents required by PRI" and "all agreements which PRI may require," with no standard limiting what PRI may demand. That unbounded discretion can defeat the termination remedy the subsection is meant to implement.

This tolling sentence excludes only November and December from the computation, while the parallel tolling paragraph following 5.01(d) excludes October, November and December. The inconsistent exclusions in otherwise identical machinery invite argument about which applies.

The "Release Territories" are listed as including "Benelux" and "Scandinavia," neither of which is defined, and paragraph 7.03(c) separately names only Sweden and Denmark among Scandinavian countries. Whether Norway or Finland is a Release Territory cannot be answered from the text.

PRI undertakes to instruct its licensees not to manufacture competing Records but then disclaims liability "by reason of such manufacture at any time," cancelling the duty just imposed. The sentence also makes the instruction depend on notice from the licensee rather than from Grantor.

PRI's "continuing right at all times" to manufacture and sell recompilation Albums is expressed as subject only to paragraph 5.01(b)(ix)(B), and so appears to override the three-Album cap on "Greatest Hits" compilations in 5.01(b)(ix)(A). The two provisions cannot both be given full effect.

This tolling sentence excludes October, November and December, while the corresponding tolling sentence at the end of paragraph 5.01(c) excludes only November and December. The discrepancy between the two identical mechanisms requires construction.

PRI is given the "exclusive right" to utilize Artist's performances in Audio-Visual Recordings, yet paragraph 5.02(b) forbids either party to produce or exploit a Concert Video without the other's consent. The exclusive grant and the mutual-consent limitation cannot both stand as written.

The sentence attaches the condition "but only if ... the immediately preceding Album ... has either achieved Net Sales ... of one hundred thousand (100,000) units ... or has been entered in the 'Top 75' Billboard" after listing both first and second Albums, so it is unclear whether the condition qualifies only the second Albums or both. Whether PRI owes a Video for a first Album turns on that reading.

Artist "waives any right to receive such compensation to the extent that such right may be waived" under the applicable collective bargaining agreement — a self-referential waiver whose scope depends on documents outside the contract. What, if anything, is actually payable is not determinable from the provision.

The mutual-consent regime for Concert Videos conflicts with paragraph 5.02(a)(i), which grants PRI the exclusive right to exploit Artist's performances in Audio-Visual Recordings for commercial purposes. Paragraph 8(b) of the 1989 amendment then purports to free PRI of 5.02(b) for one Concert Video, sharpening the question of what 5.02(b) still governs.

Grantor must procure an "irrevocable written consent" from the proprietor of each non-Controlled Composition for recording and promotional use "without payment," a result Grantor may have no power to deliver, while payment terms for commercial use are left to future good-faith negotiation. The obligation and the open negotiation sit uneasily together.

The power of attorney is triggered if Grantor "unreasonably refuses to do so and/or fails to return the same to PRI within ten (10) days" — the "and/or" leaves it unclear whether unreasonableness is required at all or mere delay suffices. That determines whether PRI can sign in Grantor's name over a reasonable objection.

PRI is given the perpetual right to use Artist's name and likeness "in connection with other merchandising of any kind," while paragraph 5.04(c) expressly reserves to Grantor the right to exploit those same rights "in all forms of merchandising" notwithstanding anything to the contrary. The two grants cover the same subject matter and conflict.

Grantor's approval right over unsupplied likenesses and different biographical material is negated by the closing sentence that "any inadvertent failure by PRI to obtain the aforesaid approval shall not be deemed a breach." What content "inadvertent" has, and whether the approval right is enforceable at all, is left open.

Grantor's reservation of merchandising rights "notwithstanding anything to the contrary expressed or implied herein" cannot be squared with paragraph 5.04(a), which grants PRI perpetual rights to use the same names and likenesses in merchandising of any kind. Which reservation controls is the construction question.

The clause identifying Grantor's "current arrangement" with a named merchandiser is illegible/blank in the executed text, and the condition "provided PRI at the time has in the past and can arrange a 'first-class' merchandising activity" is ungrammatical. Both the counterparty and the condition to PRI's Matching Right are therefore indeterminate.

The Matching Right revives if the third-party agreement is "not so consummated" with the same parties, but no time limit or definition of consummation is given. How long Grantor's freedom to contract lasts after PRI declines is unstated.

The balance of the initial Advance is payable on receipt of the agreement "fully executed by Grantor and Artist," yet the preamble names only PolyGram and DeNovo as parties, so it is unclear in what capacity Artist's execution is required. Whether payment was ever due turns on that.

The Album-by-Album Advance schedule in 6.01(b) was deleted in its entirety and replaced by paragraph 6 of the 1989 amendment, which sets materially different amounts (e.g. $200,000 rather than $225,000 for the Second Album) and adds a Ninth Album. Which schedule governs any given Album must be construed across the two documents.

Grantor is made responsible for "all Recording Costs," but paragraph 3.02 puts the scheduling and booking of all studio time in PRI's hands unless Grantor furnishes a studio letter looking only to Grantor for payment. Who bears costs PRI incurs when it does the booking is not resolved between the two.

The Advance reduction runs from the "Final Date," defined as the last date the Album would be timely delivered under paragraph 4.01, but 4.01(d)(i) says delivery within sixty days after the 4.01(a)/(b) dates is not a failure to comply. Whether the Final Date includes that sixty-day cushion decides when the ten-percent-per-month reduction begins.

The Greatest Hits Advance is payable only if the royalty account is "in a recouped position" as of the accounting period preceding release, a status computed by PRI on figures it alone holds. The definition supplied in parentheses does not say how reserves held under 8.01 affect that computation.

The sweeping deeming of "any monies other than royalties paid to Grantor during the Term" as Advances cannot be squared with paragraph 6.04(b), which declares half of the $160,000 tour support non-returnable, non-recoupable and "not Advances under this agreement." The overlap between the two must be construed.

This paragraph deems half of the video production costs of the first two Audio-Visual Recordings per Album to be Advances, while paragraph 5.02(a)(ii) says that notwithstanding 6.03 none of the production costs of Audio-Visual Recordings in excess of two are recoupable. Read with 8.01's bar on recouping video costs "except as set forth in paragraph 6.03," the recoupable amount is uncertain.

Cross-collateralization is stated to reach Advances under "any recording agreement between Grantor and Polydor K.K. ... and/or amendment(s) thereto," without identifying the agreements or limiting them to those existing at signature. The scope of the "Polydor Agreements" being cross-collateralized is the ambiguous term.

One-half of the tour support is deemed "non-returnable, non-recoupable" and not an Advance, which pulls directly against paragraph 6.02's rule that any non-royalty monies paid to Grantor are Advances and against the cross-collateralization in 6.04(a). Whether the other half remains recoupable under the Polydor Agreements as well as here is unresolved.

The proviso that no royalties accrue or become payable "until such time as all Advances ... have been repaid to PRI" uses repayment language for what the rest of the contract treats as recoupment from royalties, and paragraph 8.01 provides for payment of accrued royalties "less Advances or other recoupable amounts." Whether "repaid" means cash repayment or recoupment is the ambiguity.

The eleven-percent rate applies to Albums "sold by PRI for distribution through Normal Retail Channels in the United States," but paragraph 7.06(a) accrues fifty percent of net receipts on licenses of the Master Recordings to third parties. Which provision governs a given exploitation — a sale through a distributor or a license to a third party — is the contest the two provisions set up.

The escalation applies "For Net Sales ... in excess of one hundred thousand (100,000) units," without saying whether the higher rate applies only to units above the threshold or retroactively to all units. The reach of "in excess of" is the ambiguity.

Like 7.02(b), this escalation says the rate "shall be thirteen percent ... in lieu of" the base rate for sales "in excess of" 250,000 units, leaving open whether the new rate applies to all units or only the excess. It also does not say whether the escalations are cumulative across accounting periods.

The 500,000-unit escalation repeats the "in excess of ... in lieu of" formula without specifying whether the higher rate reaches all units sold or only those above the threshold. The sentence is also mangled ("in the States of any Album ... United"), obscuring the territory qualifier.

The 750,000-unit escalation uses the same undefined "in excess of ... in lieu of" formula, leaving the calculation base for the fifteen-percent rate open. Whether it displaces the lower escalations prospectively or retroactively is unstated.

The fourteen-percent Japanese rate must be read against paragraph 6.04(a), which cross-collateralizes with recording agreements between Grantor and Polydor K.K., the Japanese company. Whether Japanese sales are accounted under this paragraph or under the Polydor Agreements is not settled by either text.

The UK/Canada rate is three-fourths of "the otherwise applicable royalty rate in the United States," while 7.03(e) says the 7.02 escalations do not apply — leaving unclear whether the base is the 11% rate of 7.02(a) or some escalated rate. The referent of "otherwise applicable" is the ambiguity.

The two-thirds foreign rate again keys to "the otherwise applicable royalty rate in the United States" without identifying which US rate, and the territory list omits countries covered by "Scandinavia" and "Benelux" in the Release Territories of 5.01(d). Whether a sale in Norway falls here or under 7.03(d) is open.

The rest-of-world rate is half of "the otherwise applicable royalty rate in the United States," a referent that 7.03(e)'s exclusion of escalations makes uncertain. The provision also does not say how it interacts with the configuration reductions in 7.05.

PRI's option, "at its sole discretion," between a dollars-and-cents equivalent royalty and a percentage royalty refers in one branch to "compact disc or other new Record configuration" and in the other only to compact discs, leaving unclear whether the option extends to configurations invented later. What counts as an "other new Record configuration" is the term at issue.

The provision is an agreement to "negotiate in good faith" over a compact disc royalty adjustment "taking into account industry-wide standards," with no formula and no consequence if agreement is never reached. Whether it creates any enforceable obligation is the question.

The half-rate applies to "premium Records, Budget Records, or Records other than Albums not otherwise specifically referred to herein" — a catch-all that on its face swallows configurations given their own rates elsewhere, such as Singles under 7.01 and the EP and Long-Play Single rates in 7.05(b). Whether the general words are cut down by the specific rates is the ejusdem generis problem.

The two-thirds rate for EP Records, Mid-Price Records and Long-Play Singles overlaps the half-rate in 7.05(a) for "Records other than Albums not otherwise specifically referred to herein," and a Long-Play Single answers both descriptions. Which rate applies to overlapping configurations is unresolved between the two subparagraphs.

The three-fourths Armed Forces rate does not say how it combines with the other reductions — a Budget Record sold in a post exchange falls within both 7.05(a) and 7.05(c). Whether the reductions stack or one displaces the other is unstated.

The Multiple-Record Album formula is expressed as "subject to the terms of paragraph 3.06," which deems any multiple LP Album a single LP "for the purposes of product delivery and payment therefor." Whether the fractional royalty formula or 3.06's single-LP deeming controls payment is the conflict.

The fifty-percent net-receipts rate is tied to enumerated categories closing with "or by any combination of the methods set forth above or other methods" and "licenses of Master Recordings on a flat-fee basis," so whether a modern third-party distribution licence falls inside the list is a general-versus-specific question. The catch-all sits directly against the enumerated channels.

If an exploitation is a "license of Master Recordings" under 7.06(a) it pays fifty percent of net receipts, but if it is a "Net Sale" it pays the far lower percentage rates in 7.02 and 7.05; the same transaction can be characterised either way. The two royalty regimes cannot both apply and the contract does not say which prevails.

"Net receipts" permits deduction of "any costs or expenses or amounts which PRI is obligated to pay to third parties, such as, without limitation," followed by examples — an open-ended deduction with no boundary. What may be netted out before the fifty-percent split is the ambiguity.

The record-club rate turns on clubs "operated by parties affiliated with PRI," a term left undefined and standing against the "Non-Affiliated Third Party" clubs in 7.06(a)(i) that pay fifty percent of net receipts. Which side of the line a club falls on decides a large rate difference.

A five-percent rate for sales by "PRI's affiliated licensees" through direct mail and key outlet marketing sits against paragraph 7.06(a)(ii), which pays fifty percent of net receipts for the identical channels when the licensee is non-affiliated. Whether a given licensee is "affiliated" is undefined and decisive.

The division by the number of royalty-earning artists overlaps the pro-ration in paragraph 7.10 for Records not consisting entirely of Master Recordings hereunder, so a joint recording on a mixed Record could be reduced twice. Whether the two reductions compound is unresolved.

The pro-ration by number of Master Recordings can apply on top of the division among royalty-earning artists in 7.09 for the same Record. Neither provision says whether the reductions are alternative or cumulative.

Paragraph 8.01 provides for payment of accrued royalties "less Advances or other recoupable amounts," while the opening of Article 7 states that no royalties accrue or become payable until all Advances "have been repaid to PRI." The two accounting rules describe different mechanics for the same money.

Royalties are computed "in the same national currency as PRI is accounted to by its licensees" and are not payable until PRI is paid in United States Dollars, with a deduction permitted proportionate to any restriction on the licensee's remittances. Whether that lets PRI defer or reduce royalties indefinitely on foreign sales is left open.

Statements become binding unless objected to within three years "from the date rendered," while paragraph 8.05(a) allows four years from the same date to sue — so a claim can be timely as a suit but foreclosed as an objection. The relation between the two limits requires construction.

Statements are "deemed conclusively to have been rendered on the due date" unless Grantor objects within thirty days, so the limitation clocks in 8.03(a) and 8.05(a) can run on statements never actually sent. Whether a statement never received can be "rendered" is the defect.

The audit right covers "the six (6) accounting periods prior to such audit" but may be exercised "only within three (3) years after the date when PRI is required to send" the statement, and six semi-annual periods is itself three years — so the two limits give inconsistent reach. Which controls a statement rendered late is unclear.

The opening words are garbled — "Notwithstanding the last sentence of paragraph 8.04(a), ~, PQI notifies Grantor" — so the conditional trigger ("if PRI notifies") is not actually stated. The mechanical error obscures when the suspension right arises.

Grantor's examination must be "commenced within thirty (30) days" of delivery of the final report on the Other Examination and "conducted in a reasonably continuous manner," without saying what happens if it is not. Whether these are conditions forfeiting the audit right or mere covenants is unstated.

The four-year suit limit runs from the date the statement "was rendered," but under 8.03(b) statements are deemed conclusively rendered on the due date whether or not sent. The limitation period can therefore expire on statements Grantor never received.

The clause purports to strip the court of "authority to consider any other issues or award any relief except recovery of any royalties found owing" on "any claim related to PRI's royalty accountings," then reopens everything if a court finds "fraud or gross negligence." Both the reach of "related to" and the self-referential fraud exception require construction.

Controlled Compositions are licensed at "the Statutory Rate prevailing at the time of release in the applicable country," yet Canada is included, where no United States statutory rate exists, and no per-Album cap or freeze date is stated in this subparagraph. What rate applies in Canada, and at what date, is the ambiguity.

Royalty-bearing free goods are defined by reference to "paragraph 13.15(a)(ii) below," a provision not contained in this instrument as executed. The mechanical royalty base cannot be computed without the missing cross-referenced definition.

Arrangements of public domain compositions are royalty-free unless the arranged version "varies substantially from the original work," a standard with no defined threshold. Payment then depends on "documentation satisfactory to PRI" of the ASCAP/BMI ratio, a further unmeasured condition.

The subparagraph breaks off mid-sentence at "Mechanical royalty reserves maintained by PRI against anticipated returns," so the liquidation terms for mechanical reserves are missing from the instrument. Unlike the royalty reserves in 8.01, no liquidation schedule limits how long PRI may hold them.
